papers.title_in_file: Parameterized quantum circuits as universal generative models for continuous multivariate distributions
papers.version_note: The text is arXiv:2402.09848v2 of 29 May 2024. The title in the text differs from the title words in the file name (Expressivity of parameterized quantum circuits for generative modeling of ...); the arXiv number 2402.09848 in the file name matches the text.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proves expectation value samplers built from parameterized quantum circuits are universal generative models for multivariate distributions and gives necessary conditions on qubits and observable norm.

existing.note: Confirmed. The paper does give a weaker non-simulatability argument before this sentence (see the new assertion on BQP and BPP); the stored value is about the stronger arguments only and is right as stored.
existing.value: The authors state that stronger advantage arguments for expectation value samplers, in which no polynomial-time randomized Turing machine can sample the output distribution under standard assumptions, are left for future work.
quotes: It may be possible to construct stronger advantage arguments where we find the existence of an expectation value sampler
such that its output distribution cannot be sampled by any polynomial-time randomized Turing machine (subject to standard assumptions) but we leave this for future work.

existing.note: Narrowed. The necessary conditions bound the number of qubits against the output dimension and the observable spectral norm. The link to the number of measurements is made by a lemma whose proof assumes a simplified Gaussian shot-noise model, and the paper states that the dense encoding family is not optimal against the Holevo-based condition. Anchor check: the quoted necessary-conditions sentence is in Section VI and the trade-off sentence is in Section I; neither is in the abstract text. The abstract says 'tight bounds', which the body supports only for the product encoding endpoint.
existing.value: The paper proves necessary conditions that bound the number of qubits against the output dimension and the observable spectral norm, and it links the observable norm to the number of measurements through a lemma proved under a simplified Gaussian shot-noise model; the authors state that this shows a trade-off between the number of measurements and the number of qubits, and that the dense encoding family is not optimal with respect to the Holevo-based condition, leaving a quasi-quadratic gap.

existing.note: Narrowed. Universality is for convergence in distribution on the bounded support [−1, 1]M, and each design has a stated resource cost. Anchor check: the quote 'We provide constructive proofs for two extremal circuit designs.' is in Section VI, not in the abstract text.
existing.value: The paper proves that expectation value samplers based on parameterized quantum circuits are universal generative models, in the sense of convergence in distribution, for target densities with support included in [−1, 1]M , with constructive proofs for two extremal designs: a product encoding design with n = M qubits and unit norm observables, and a dense encoding design with a number of qubits in Θ(log M ) and observable spectral norm in Θ(M ); each is stated as approximating the target to within epsilon in the Wasserstein distance.

assertions.value: The paper defines an expectation value sampling model on n qubits by a parameterized quantum circuit that takes data as input and returns a unitary matrix, a vector of M observables, and an input distribution; the model output is a sample of the vector of expectation values of the observables on the circuit state, drawn when the input follows the input distribution.
quotes: An expectation value sampling model on n qubits is defined by (Uθ, O, pX ), where Uθ : X ⊆ RL → U (2n) is a parameterized quantum circuit taking data as input and returning a unitary matrix,
is a vector of M observables, and pX : X ⊆ RL → R is the input distribution.
The output of the model is a sample drawn from the distribution pY with Y = f (X) ∼ pY when X ∼ pX .
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 1 in Section II A.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike in the quantum circuit Born machine, the randomness of an expectation value sampler comes from the classical random input to the circuit and not from the measurement process, and that expectation value samplers have continuous support.
quotes: It is important to note that, in contrast to the quantum circuit Born machine, the randomness does not come from the measurement process, but from the classical randomness provided as an input to the quantum circuit.
Notably, unlike QCBMs, expectation value samplers have continuous support (absolutely continuous random variables, see Definition 6).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II A states the model setup.

assertions.value: The paper defines a generative model as universal if for every probability density function on the support there is a sequence of densities from the model whose random variables converge in distribution to the target, and states that this is equivalent to pointwise convergence of the cumulative distribution functions.

distribution functions of pk, which we call Pk, converges pointwise to the cumulative distribution function of q,

assertions.value: The authors sketch a construction of an invertible mapping from the uniform random variable to an absolutely continuous random variable on a bounded box, built from inverse cumulative distribution functions of the marginal and of the successive conditionals, and state that the resulting mapping is bounded and piece-wise continuous; the construction excludes distributions such as Dirac deltas.

assertions.value: The paper states as a theorem that if a family of mappings is dense in the set of all functions in the pointwise convergence topology, then this family together with an input probability density with non zero support yields a universal generative model family; it derives this from the sufficient condition, attributed to Kobyzev et al., that density in the set of monotonically increasing functions suffices.
quotes: From [KPB21], it is sufficient for a family of mappings to be dense in the set of all monotonically increasing functions in the pointwise convergence topology to yield a universal generative model.
Theorem 1. If a family of mappings G = {g : X ⊆ RM → Y ⊆ RM } is dense in the set of all functions in the pointwise convergence topology,
then this family of mappings G together with a probability density function pX with non zero support on X yields a universal generative model family on Y (cf Definition 2).
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 is stated with its conditions in Section II C; the proof is a one-line deduction from the cited sufficient condition.
assertions.reader_inference: The result rests on the cited condition from Kobyzev et al. The paper later uses it with density only in the piecewise continuous functions (Theorem 2), which is narrower than the 'all functions' printed here.

assertions.value: The authors state that n-qubit expectation value samplers with constant observable norm are universal for M-dimensional distributions with constant support radius, for M equal to n, and that the size of the cube can be rescaled by rescaling the norm of the observables.

assertions.value: The paper states as a theorem that for an n-qubit expectation value sampling model to approximate any distribution with support in [−1, 1]M to any accuracy epsilon greater than zero, it is necessary that M is at most four to the power n minus one.

assertions.value: The authors argue that any observable on a single qubit is a linear combination of the three Pauli matrices, so a single qubit expectation value sampler has at most three degrees of independence, and that for M greater than three universality is impossible because the four-dimensional uniform distribution cannot be approximated.
quotes: Indeed, any observable can be expressed as a linear combination of the three Pauli matrices.
Therefore the distribution output by a single qubit expectation value sampler will have at most three degrees of independence, and for M > 3 it is impossible to have
universality because it is impossible to approximate e.g. the 4-dimensional uniform distribution.
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument in the text.

Using Lemma 7.1.10 from [AGS05], we know that the Wasserstein distance between pY and pYˆ , Wp(pY , pYˆ ) ∈ O(ϵ).
For simplicity, we consider a vanilla estimation where each observable with norm ∥O∥ is measured t times and the average is returned.

assertions.reader_inference: The text says standard deviation epsilon, writes the covariance as epsilon times the identity, and then sets epsilon squared in Θ(∥O∥/t); these conventions are not reconciled in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Gaussian shot-noise analysis cannot trivially be applied to techniques such as shadow tomography, because the corresponding shot noise cannot in general be modelled by independent Gaussian noise, since the covariance matrix will in general not be proportional to the identity.
quotes: Note that the first result cannot be trivially applied to techniques such as shadow tomography [CKWD]. Indeed the corresponding shot noise ρ cannot in general be modelled by a Gaussian independent noise, at the least the covariance matrix will in general not be proportional to the identity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the observable spectral norm relates to the number of measurements needed to approximate it up to an additive accuracy, that this highlights a trade-off between the number of qubits and the number of measurements, or space versus time complexity, and that applying the measurement lemma to the product and dense encoding circuits shows this trade-off.
assertions.anchor: Sections IV C and IV D, pp.5-6
quotes: In practice, the observable spectral norm relates to the number of measurements required to approximate it up to an additive accuracy.
This highlights a trade-off between the number of qubits and the number of measurements, or space versus time complexity, which we formalize in the next subsection.
This lemma can be applied to both the product encoding circuit and the dense encoding circuit to show the trade-off between the number of qubits and the number of measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: The trade-off rests on the measurement lemma proved under a simplified noise model.

assertions.value: The abstract states that the authors explore various architectures which allow universality and prove tight bounds connecting the minimal required qubit number and the minimal required number of measurements needed.
quotes: We explore various architectures which allow universality and prove tight bounds connecting the minimal required qubit number, and the minimal required number of measurements needed.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract claim that the body qualifies.
assertions.reader_inference: The body shows optimality for the product encoding endpoint only; it states a quasi-quadratic gap for the dense encoding and leaves intermediate optimal families as a conjecture.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantity driving the necessary conditions is the number of independent variables M′ rather than the dimension M of the target distribution, that the proofs use M equal to M′ because universality is defined to include full independence, and that restricting to classes of distributions with dependence conditions can give much more economic bounds.
quotes: It is interesting to note that the parameter driving the necessary conditions is not the dimension of the target distribution itself M but rather the number of independent variables M ′.
Because we defined universality as being able to capture full independence we use M = M ′ in the proofs of the necessary conditions.

However, by restricting our interest to universality for classes of distributions with certain dependence conditions fulfilled, we can obtain much more economic bounds than for the general case, which is illustrated in Figure 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a remark without a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that for M-dimensional distributions with support in a 2-dimensional linear subspace, the circuit of the cited one-qubit universal approximant work together with two observables gives a universal generator on one qubit for any target dimension M.
quotes: First, consider the family of distributions that are M dimensional but that have their support included in a 2-dimensional linear subspace.

We choose the expectation value sam√pler a√s the circuit from [PSLNGS+21] and observables { 2X, 2Z} we have a universal generator on one qubit for this 2-linear family for any target distribution dimension M .
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an example without a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer drops radical signs; the observables are printed as { 2X, 2Z}, which are read as the square root of two times X and Z.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the family of M-dimensional Dirichlet distributions, with positive coordinates summing to unity, the dense encoding circuit with n = log M qubits, taking raw probabilities as observables instead of amplified probabilities, constitutes a universal model, with exponentially fewer qubits than the general case.
quotes: Second, consider the family of M -dimensional Dirichlet distributions, for which each coordinate is positive, and such that the sum of all coordinates is unity.
For this case, we can take the “dense encoding” circuit with n = log M qubits, see Figure 3, and instead of amplified probabilities we take the raw probabilities as observables.
This constitutes a universal model for the Dirichlet family.
In this case, we get away with exponentially fewer qubits than the general case.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an example without a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: Section II B treats universality on the 1-norm unit simplex as the Dirichlet case, so Dirichlet here appears to mean distributions on the simplex.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that their observations may indicate that expectation value samplers are better suited to generate highly correlated distributions, and note that for the Dirichlet case the normalization condition matches the normalization of quantum states.
quotes: These observations may be used to suggest that expectation value samplers are better suited to generate highly correlated distributions.
making this type of universality particularly well suited to expectation value samplers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A suggestion by the authors, not a result.

assertions.value: The paper defines the primary mapping of an n-qubit encoding circuit as the mapping of the expectation value sampling model with the Pauli basis as observables, yielding a random variable of dimension four to the power n, and writes any vector of M observables as a matrix applied to the vector of all Pauli strings.
quotes: Any vector of M observables O = (Om), can be expressed as a linear mapping applied on the vector of all Pauli strings: O = AP, where A is an M ×4n matrix, and P is a 4n dimensional vector.

Definition 4 (Primary mapping). The primary mapping g of an n-qubit encoding circuit Uθ(x) is defined as the mapping of the associated expectation value sampling model with the Pauli basis P, defined as (Uθ(x), P, pX ) according to Definition 1.
It yields the 4n-dimensional random variable Z = g(X) when X ∼ pX .
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 4 in Section V A.
assertions.reader_inference: Equation (9) prints the index range as 1≤k≤2n while the text says four to the power n dimensions; the exponents are flat in the text layer, so this reads as a typographic slip.

assertions.value: The paper states as a theorem that, for a given encoding circuit and input distribution, the expectation value sampling model with any choice of observables is a linear transformation of the model with the Pauli basis.
quotes: Theorem 7. Given an encoding circuit Uθ(x) and random variable with distribution pX , for any the choice of observables O, the expectation value sampling model
(Uθ(x), O, pX ) (according to Definition 1) is a linear transformation of the expectation value sampling model
(Uθ(x), P, pX ), where P is the Pauli basis per definition of the primary mapping in Definition 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 7 is stated with its conditions; it follows from writing the observables in the Pauli basis.

assertions.value: The paper states as a lemma that, for an encoding circuit on n qubits and an input distribution, any expectation value model using them yields at most L uncorrelated variables, where L is the number of non-zero eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the primary mapping, and that L is at most four to the power n minus one.
quotes: Lemma 3. Given an encoding circuit U (x) over n qubits and random variable with distribution pX , we note L the number of non-zero eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the primary mapping.
For any choice of observables, any expectation value model using (U (x), pX ) will yield at most L uncorrelated variables. In addition L ≤ 4n − 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 3 is stated with its conditions and follows from Theorem 7.

A generalized chaos expansion is a representation of a random variable Y with probability density pY as a vector α in this Hilbert space, such that:

assertions.value: The authors state that one of the main results of polynomial chaos expansion is that such expansions are universal generative models.
quotes: In particular, one of the main results of polynomial chaos expansion is that they are universal generative models.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to prior work without a pointer to the theorem.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing Schuld et al., that quantum reuploading circuits that use an integer-valued spectrum Hamiltonian have an output hypothesis function that can be decomposed as an exact finite Fourier series.
quotes: It has been widely studied and used that if they use integer-valued spectrum Hamiltonian, their output hypothesis function can be decomposed as an exact finite Fourier series [SSM21].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper states as a theorem that any expectation value sampling model using a quantum reuploading model with integer-valued spectrum, together with the uniform distribution on [0, 2π)M, outputs a random variable that has an exact finite polynomial chaos expansion for any choice of observables.
quotes: Theorem 8. Any expectation value sampling model using a quantum reuploading model with integer-valued spectrum Uθ(x),
together with the uniform distribution on [0, 2π)M outputs a random variable Y that has an exact finite polynomial chaos expansion for any choice of observables.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper gives no proof beyond extending the cited Fourier series fact.

assertions.value: The authors state that many properties of such models are expected to transfer from the regression context to the generative context beyond universality, but they leave that for future work.
quotes: Therefore it is expected that, beyond the universality, many properties of such models can be transferred from a regressive context to a generative context, but we leave that for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this as left for future work.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, because common parameterized quantum circuits are periodic, a Gaussian input to an expectation value sampler would map a highest probability input and a very low probability input to the same output sample, and that this supports choosing the uniform distribution as input, in contrast to classical GANs where Gaussians are typically preferred.
quotes: Indeed, it is known that the most commonly used parameterized quantum circuits are periodic, in particular when they have a finite Fourier decomposition.
X = 0 is the highest probability event and will yield the exact same output as a very low probability event, for example, X = 100.
This choice of uniform distribution is in contrast to classical GANs where Gaussians are typically preferred.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by example in the text.

assertions.value: The paper recalls, from Pérez-Salinas et al., that for any continuous function of the input into the unit interval, any continuous phase function and any epsilon, there exists a one qubit circuit whose amplitude on the one state is uniformly within epsilon of the function times a phase.
quotes: We start by recalling Theorem 4 from [PSLNGS+21],
There exists a one qubit circuit U : [0, 1]M → U(2) s.t.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper proves as a theorem that for any continuous function from the unit cube into the interval [−1, 1] and any epsilon, there exists a one qubit circuit and an observable with unit spectral norm whose expectation value is within epsilon of the function for every input, which gives uniform density of quantum functions in the bounded continuous functions.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 10 and proof, Appendix B, p.10
quotes: Theorem 10. For any function g ∈ C([0, 1]M → [−1, 1])
and for any ϵ > 0, there exists a one qubit circuit U (x) : [0, 1]M → U (2) and an observable O with unit spectral norm ∥O∥ = 1 s.t.
This yields the uniform density of quantum functions in the set of bounded continuous functions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 10 is stated with its conditions and proved in Appendix B from the cited Theorem 9.

assertions.value: The paper states as a theorem that for any bounded piecewise continuous function from the unit cube into [−1, 1] there is a sequence of one qubit circuits with observables of unit spectral norm whose functions converge pointwise to it; it builds this on the preceding uniform-density theorem and the cited result that bounded piecewise continuous functions are of Baire class one.
quotes: In particular in [Lac84, Leb04], it was proven that bounded piecewise continuous functions are of class 1.
Theorem 11. For any function f : B([0, 1]M → [−1, 1]), there exists a sequence (indexed by k) of one qubit circuit
and observables with unit spectral norm,
converges pointwise to f .
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 11 is stated with its conditions and follows from Theorem 10 and the cited Baire class result.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is split across a page break in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that they did not address whether it is a good idea to use expectation value samplers, that quantum advantage cannot be proven for them as easily as for quantum circuit Born machines, and that the hardness of simulating them does not connect straightforwardly to hardness-of-sampling results from quantum supremacy.
quotes: While we characterized important properties of expectation value samplers, we did not address the question of whether it is a good idea to use them.
Expectation value samplers cannot be proven to be a path for certain types of quantum advantage as easily as is the case in Quantum Circuit Born Machines [CMDK20].
hardness-ofsampling results established in the domain of quantum supremacy results [CMDK20].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limits of their own work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming BQP is not in BPP, there is no polynomial time algorithm that takes the classical description of an arbitrary expectation value sampler and outputs a sample from a distribution epsilon close to its output, and give as an example a hard-to-simulate circuit that does not depend on the input data, which yields a Dirac delta distribution that classical samplers could efficiently sample but cannot easily be found from the circuit description.
quotes: Assuming BQP is not in BPP, there exists no polynomial time algorithm that takes a classical description of an arbitrary expectation value sampler A as an input and outputs a sample from a distribution that is epsilon close to that of the output of A.

This yields a Dirac delta distribution for which there exist classical samplers to efficiently sample from it, however, such classical samplers cannot be easily found based on the classical description of the expectation value sampler.
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument stated without a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument is about simulating an arbitrary sampler given its description, not about a fixed sampler.

assertions.value: The authors state that the expressivity and universality of quantum Born machines have been clarified in cited work, whereas expectation value sampling models are not so well understood, and that the output dimension of an expectation value sampler is not inherently tied to the number of qubits.
quotes: While for quantum Born machines, the expressivity and universality have been clarified [LW18, CMDK20], in contrast, expectation value sampling models are not so well understood.
In particular, an interesting feature of expectation value sampling is that the dimension of the output is not inherently tied to the number of qubits used.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of motivation with citations to other work.
